title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say
description: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local aut
body: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say

title: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
description: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donal
body: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump."The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship. "Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote."If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her -  or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated."Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC. "The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe." Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation". But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago. Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

schema.headline: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'

title: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
description: Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have b
body: Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have been a deliberate attack. The independent MP, 65, was struck outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria, on Monday afternoon.A man, 43, from the nearby town of Tarrawingee was detained at the scene by a passerby and police say a knife was found in the car.Police are investigating whether it was an "intentional act" but say they do not believe there is an "ongoing threat to the community".Political leaders have expressed shock and dismay, with Albanese saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy".   While Albanese said it was too early to understand the motive behind what had happened, he did say the political temperature had been rising in Australia. His Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke backed up that statement with figures showing that reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 in the past year.Haines was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at 15:35 (04:35 GMT) outside her office on Murphy Street in Wangaratta, police say.The town, which has a population of around 30,000, is a few hours north-east of Melbourne.A witness told Australian broadcaster ABC they had heard a bang and seen a woman pinned between two cars, external.Haines was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta but later moved to Melbourne by helicopter.After being subdued and detained by the passersby, the suspect was arrested by police. Announcing that counter terror police were involved in the investigation, the prime minister said: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."In a statement, Victoria Police said: "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act."It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other... The investigation remains ongoing."Although not necessarily a household name across Australia, in the political sphere Helen Haines is both well-known and well regarded as an anti-corruption campaigner.There has been an outpouring of messages from politicians and party leaders across the breadth of the political spectrum. In an age of increasingly divisive politics, she is seen by many as a unifying force.The independent MP has only been a federal parliamentarian for a relatively short time, having been elected in 2019. However, in that time she has become an influential advocate for integrity in politics.Haines proposed legislation for a national anti-corruption watchdog in 2021, and has been credited for driving the creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission under Labor in the previous parliamentary term.She currently sits on the parliamentary committee responsible for its oversight.Haines has often banded together with other key independents on issues that include climate action and gender equality.Allegra Spender, another independent MP who has collaborated with Haines, called her "the best of us".

schema.headline: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack

title: Erling Haaland doubt, Antoine Semenyo injured: Who could play for Man City against AEK Athens?
description: Haaland has scored in six consecutive top-flight games to help City to the top of the table with a flawless start from their opening seven games of th
body: Haaland has scored in six consecutive top-flight games to help City to the top of the table with a flawless start from their opening seven games of the campaign.Against Ipswich, he scored his 100th non-penalty goal in the Premier League, reaching this milestone in fewer appearances than any other player.Maresca said Haaland "can be available" against AEK and will be assessed after training on Monday, but the player was not present during the session which was open to the media.Players can find it difficult to feature as back-ups to Haaland, as Julian Alvarez and Omar Marmoush have found in the past, but it was a surprise when Divin Mubama was allowed to join Championship side Southampton on loan in the summer.It left City without a natural replacement in Haaland's absence.Maresca has previously said Semenyo can be used "as a nine" but that plan is no longer available with the Ghanaian facing the prospect of missing up to 13 matches.One option mooted by the Italian is midfielder Phil Foden, who ended his barren run in front of goal on Saturday by scoring his first Premier League goal since December."Phil can be one of the solutions," said Maresca. "He played already in the past in that position so could play again, but at the moment the number nine is Erling."Could summer signing Iliman Ndiaye be another option?The Senegal international was often deployed as a striker in Sheffield United's promotion-winning campaign in 2022-23, scoring 14 goals to help the Blades return to the Premier League.Last season, manager Pep Guardiola said Rayan Cherki fits playing in the false nine role "perfectly", with the Frenchman scoring in a 2-0 Carabao Cup quarter-final win over Brentford when used in that position.

schema.headline: Erling Haaland doubt, Antoine Semenyo injured: Who could play for Man City against AEK Athens?

title: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row
description: The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.Apu Nahas
body: The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode titled The Revengening, voiced by India-born US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra.The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret.Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said.The character, who has been part of the long-running US animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent.Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes.The following year, an episode of the long-running US cartoon addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations, but some viewers found it insufficient.The Simpsons' Apu: 'A stereotype hiding in plain sight'Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes.Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise."Speaking to Variety, external ahead of the weekend's latest episode, Azaria's replacement Malhotra explained: "When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink."But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers' room look different now?"The Grey's Anatomy and The Legend of Korra actor continued: "Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologised for past mistakes?"Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn't disappoint fans?"After years of Apu having become a mere background character, Malhotra said he spoke with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos about how they could make the returning fans' favourite more culturally appropriate for 2026."It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for long-time fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way."Apu's wife, Manjula, will now be voiced Janina Gavankar, who previously appeared in Apple TV's The Morning Show and she takes over from Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille.In his haunting comeback episode, a man in a "Daft Monk" Halloween costume - a play on music duo Daft Punk - appears to be accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents.A year on he returns to wreak his revenge.Eventually he summons everyone to the Springfield City Hall, takes his helmet off and reveals that he's actually Apu.He then shares his story of having been nearly killed dozens of times, before winding up on The Island of Forgotten Garbage, where he was healed by Dr Nick."I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed," he declares.Just as he is about to set the city hall ablaze, Marge Simpson - serving as a thinly-veiled mouthpiece for the producers - intervenes, telling him: "Apu, we're so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing."Her famous bratty son Bart adds: "But we were so scared, and just didn't know what to do."Bart's father Homer then offers to sacrifice himself to save the rest of the town, reminding viewers of how important Apu has been to the town."You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands," said Homer."We took you for granted. I took you for granted."

schema.headline: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row

title: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts' batting issues exposed again as Scott Boland takes four
description: Second Test, Gqeberha (day two of five)South Africa 97-5: Bavuma 41*; Boland 4-31Australia: Yet to bat ScorecardFor much of Monday it appeared rain wo
body: Second Test, Gqeberha (day two of five)South Africa 97-5: Bavuma 41*; Boland 4-31Australia: Yet to bat ScorecardFor much of Monday it appeared rain would deny any meaningful play taking place on day two of the second Test between South Africa and Australia.In the end, the hosts may have wished that remained the case as their top-order frailties were exposed once again in Gqeberha. With the Proteas 97-5 at the close, the balance of power in the series remains firmly with Australia.It took Australia's metronome Scott Boland only seven deliveries to add to his two wickets taken amid the rain on day one.Relentless in his line and lengths, the 37-year-old found the perfect length to drag debutant Marques Ackerman onto the front foot.Ackerman defended nicely for 38 balls but here he neither defended nor unleashed a drive. Instead, he stumbled forward and became the 85th victim of Boland's 20-Test career as he nicked through to wicketkeeper Alex Carey.Boland ended the day with 4-31 as he, once again, emphatically pushed his case.That Ackerman, one of two batting changes from their first-Test defeat, was opening the batting against the red ball for the first time in his career pointed to the issues South Africa face.The other new face, Matthew Breetzke, was brought in on the back of his white-ball form after Tristan Stubbs played two poor strokes in the first Test. Breetzke's feet barely moved in making four from 17. He was eventually dismissed trying to force Mitchell Starc loosely through the covers off the back foot.A result of Ackerman's selection was Ryan Rickelton, another fine white-ball player with a modest red-ball record, being moved from opener to number six and wicketkeeper. After top-edging a pull last week, he was worked over by Pat Cummins' bouncers late on day two. He had already been hit on the body and dropped on 26 by Marnus Labuschagne when, stuck on the crease, he edged Boland while pushing tentatively outside off stump.On another day the ball would have found the turf but Matt Renshaw stuck out a  right hand at first slip and somehow scooped the ball up above the ground.Boland's Test bowling average now stands at 18.08. No bowler since the First World War has taken as many wickets at a better rate.His probing has ensured Australia have not missed spinner Nathan Lyon, who he replaced, or Josh Hazlewood, who remained at the team hotel throughout the day because of illness.Of Boland's 84 deliveries across this innings, 63% of his deliveries were on a good line and length, while 24% of those would have gone on to hit the stumps.On the latter metric, Cummins has the next best record but lags behind at 12%. Whether Boland has proven yet again he is ideal for seaming conditions or that he is deserving of more more opportunities can be debated. Ollie Robinson, who bowls a similar style, will surely have taken note as he prepares for England's tour of South Africa back home.With the weather set to improve, the Proteas have three days remaining in this Test to reverse the momentum of the series which only appears to be heading in one direction. Much will depend on Temba Bavuma, who remained on 41 not out, and seamer Kagiso Rabada. Rabada returned match figures of 11-150 against Australia on this ground in 2018 - a South Africa win which levelled that four-match series going into the infamous Sandpaper Test.The hosts may need similar and more here because right now their batting does not appear up to the test.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts' batting issues exposed again as Scott Boland takes four

title: Brighton: Are free-scoring Seagulls genuine Premier League title contenders?
description: When Jack Hinshelwood unapologetically smashed home Brighton and Hove Albion's fifth goal of the game against bitter rivals Crystal Palace on Sunday,
body: When Jack Hinshelwood unapologetically smashed home Brighton and Hove Albion's fifth goal of the game against bitter rivals Crystal Palace on Sunday, it completed a fourth straight Premier League win for the high-flying Seagulls - with an aggregate scoreline of 15-0.Hinshelwood's volley from two yards out to wrap up a 5-0 victory was in stark contrast to his team-mate Diego Gomez's audacious effort from the halfway line that put Brighton two up in just the seventh minute of the A23 derby.Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring side have arguably been the most entertaining top-flight team to watch this season, but they have backed up their attacking flair with a robust defence. No team has scored more and no team has conceded fewer goals.After seven games, they sit third on 16 points behind reigning champions Arsenal and table-toppers Manchester City, who have a 100% record. But can the Seagulls maintain their momentum and mount a serious title challenge?"Why not?" That's the opinion of Match of the Day pundit Dion Dublin, who played in Manchester United's 1992-93 title-winning side. "Because what we've seen of them this season is just togetherness, harmony... the manager's making good decisions."[Pascal] Gross is leading the line in regards to what goes on on the pitch and what is the right kind of way they want to play. And everybody's chipping in with goals. The look a very, very frightening team at the moment."In the summer of 2025, Brighton lost their top scorer Joao Pedro to Chelsea, and history repeated itself this year when the Blues lured veteran forward Danny Welbeck to Stamford Bridge.Once again, however, the Seagulls' enviable data-led recruitment model, aided by club owner Tony Bloom's close links to Jamestown Analytics, appears to have found a promising replacement.Having been used primarily as a substitute last season, Greece striker Charalampos Kostoulas has been entrusted to spearhead the attack, and the 19-year-old has repaid the faith shown in him by Hurzeler with three league goals and two assists.Only Lamine Yamal has more goal involvements among teenagers in Europe's top five leagues this season.Kostoulas has a strong supporting cast including Hinshelwood, Yasin Ayari, Malick Yalcouye and Maxim de Cuyper, not to mention a rejuvenated Pascal Gross pulling the strings from a deeper position.With 11 league scorers already - while also being the beneficiaries of three own goals - Hurzeler's men are sharing the load impressively. As well as being the division's top scorers, Brighton have had the most shots on target and sit second for xG, shots and big chances.In the top five European leagues, only Barcelona, with 39 goals from nine La Liga matches, have more domestic league goals than Brighton.Equally as encouraging is how well they have coped defensively despite the loss of centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke and midfield anchorman Carlos Baleba. Luka Vuskovic looks to be a tremendous acquisition from Tottenham Hotspur, and he has helped the Seagulls, who remain unbeaten at home, record a league-high five clean sheets.There are only seven previous instances of a team scoring 23 or more goals after seven games of a Premier League season. All bar one have gone on to finish in the top three, with Manchester City winning the title in 2011-12 and 2022-23.The outlier? Kevin Keegan's Newcastle United team of 1994-95, who faded and finished sixth. Comparisons have already been drawn between that side, dubbed 'The Entertainers', and the swagger of the current Brighton squad.With that in mind, Alan Wares co-host of the Albion Roar podcast suggested that perhaps a Champions League place, rather than a full-blown title challenge, might be a more realistic aim."I think with the Premier League being seven games in and the other matches we've already played, I think the dream for us is sustainability. I wouldn't go for a target, just as high as possible," said Alan."The club is really wanting to qualify for Champions League at the end of the season but yes, we've made a good start - are we title contenders? It's way too early to consider that. I would say that, at the moment, is fantasy stuff. But every football fan's got to have their dream and our point is, why not?"If we can continue this, and that is the main point we've got to look at, if we can be sustainable in what we're doing and what we achieve, then yes. Why not? Go for the sky, see what happens."With Conference League football to juggle, it seems improbable Brighton's squad can last the pace with the likes of Arsenal for the duration of the season. Leicester City, the last outsiders to lift the title, do provide some hope. They were eighth with 12 points after seven games of their memorable 2015-16 triumph.

schema.headline: Brighton: Are free-scoring Seagulls genuine Premier League title contenders?

title: Tommy Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters, trial hears
description: Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or le
body: Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or leave home, a court has heard.The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.Opening the trial, prosecutor Ben Holt said the case was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to what he perceived to be "an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday" in the aftermath of the 2024 Southport attacks.Robinson, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to the charges in July last year.Holt said Dirnhuber had to move house because of the alleged harassment, while Young was given a close protection officer by the Daily Mail after photographs of his wife and children were posted on Robinson's X account.The judge at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Justice Cavanagh, told the jury: "This is not a trial about or an assessment of the defendant's political views."Ben Holt, for the prosecution, described Yaxley-Lennon as a "well-known public figure" with a "large, vocal online following" that now included more than two million followers on social media website X.Robinson posted on X before the trial began to thank the social media platform's owner Elon Musk for funding his case – and said his court fees to date had cost him £400,000.Holt said that after the murders of three young girls in Southport on 29 July 2024, Yaxley-Lennon made a number of posts on social media. This alerted the Daily Mail and Mail Online to the fact that he was in Cyprus.The Daily Mail published articles that included photographs of the defendant, including one showing him "reclining on a sunbed using his mobile telephone".Southwark Crown Court heard that over the following days, he made a series of posts on his X account in response.On 4 August, these included: "The daily mail have purposely gave the location of where I am with my children knowing full well that people want to kill me."Another post said: "The daily mail have purposely doxed the exact location of my family. How can they be allowed to do this'."There were no identifiable pictures of Yaxley-Lennon's children published by the Daily Mail or in the Mail Online, jurors were told.Holt said the trial was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to the articles, and accused him of using "bully-boy tactics" to "intimidate" the journalists."He chose to frighten them, arrange for individuals to go to their addresses," said the prosecuting counsel."On social media — to millions of followers — he circulated images of their homes. "His supporters got involved — threatening the journalists. "Understandably, you might agree, they were scared; in some circumstances, being forced to leave their homes."The court heard that on 5 August, Dirnhuber received a number of direct messages from Robinson/Yaxley-Lennon.These included "you have endangered my children", "I'll be knocking at your door," and "let your bosses know I'm coming to all of your houses".The jury panel also heard details of an alleged phone conversation between Yaxley-Lennon and Young."He said that he had Mr Young's telephone number. He recited his home address," Mr Holt told jurors.Yaxley-Lennon then became, according to Mr Young, "increasingly menacing".The prosecutor continued: "He raised his voice, he was swearing and shouting."He said that he had been researching Mr Young's family and threatened to publish photographs of them and their addresses online."Mr Lennon told Mr Young that he would be coming to Mr Young's house and he would have to move house."He was going to shove a camera in his face and ask questions. "Mr Young told him that he did not want to engage with him — all complaints should be directed to the Daily Mail legal department."Mr Young believes Mr Lennon said 'I'm coming to get you'."

schema.headline: Tommy Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters, trial hears

title: Aberfan disaster: The portraits that helped bring the children home
description: Figure caption, The portraits which helped to bring the children of Aberfan homeByHuw ThomasBBC Wales correspondentTony Brown and Dani ThomasBBC Wales
body: Figure caption, The portraits which helped to bring the children of Aberfan homeByHuw ThomasBBC Wales correspondentTony Brown and Dani ThomasBBC WalesUpdated 19 October 2026 06:28 BSTFor almost 60 years, many of Aberfan's lost children have watched over living rooms, hallways and family gatherings across the village.Some were painted from faded school photographs. Others were shaped by the memories of grieving parents, who wrote letters to an artist describing the children they had lost: the colour of their eyes, their favourite clothes, the flashes of personality that made them unique.The portraits arrived in the years after one of Wales' darkest days. And for many families, they became far more than paintings.In a new BBC programme, Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits, some have shared their paintings and spoken about how the art helped them grieve.Image caption, The portraits helped families grieve after the Aberfan disaster"It brought her back to life," said Denise Morgan, whose younger sister Annette was among those who died in the Aberfan disaster.On 21 October 1966, a coal tip collapsed above the village. The torrent of slurry engulfed Pantglas Junior School and nearby homes, killing 144 people including 116 children.The disaster remains woven into everyday life in Aberfan. It is felt most strongly in the memorial garden on the site of the fallen school, and among the white arched monuments of the cemetery.But it is also felt in the empty places left behind at family tables, in childhood bedrooms which were suddenly occupied by one child instead of two, and in the portraits that came to represent those who never grew up.Jeanette Keane has fond memories of her sister Edwina."It was just such an idyllic childhood really," she said. "She was very quiet and gentle. She had a mischievous streak as well."The morning of the disaster remains painfully vivid, as Jeanette recalled how Edwina quickly returned home before the school day had begun."She came running back and she said, 'Mammy, I forgot to give you a kiss'," Jeanette said. "And so my mother gave her a kiss."My mother always said that, at that time, she wanted to keep her home."And my mother rued that day for the rest of her life. She just wished she'd listened to herself."Image caption, Jeanette Keane lost her sister EdwinaJeanette's father found eight-year-old Edwina trapped beneath the wreckage."She was alive," Jeanette said, but it was a heartbreaking situation."He couldn't get her out because the roof would have fallen in."The men all said, 'Teddy, you can't and my father laid by the side of her, held her hand and she suffocated."Image source, Family PhotoImage caption, Jeanette has fond memories of her sister Edwina The trauma echoed through the years that followed the disaster."It explains to me why we used to hear him walking back and fore in the corridor at night, banging his head on the wall," Jeanette said."It wasn't a very happy life afterwards. Everything changed."Image source, Bettmann Archive/Getty ImagesImage caption, The black coal waste smothered Pantglas Junior School, killing 144 people including 116 childrenDenise Morgan was attending a different school when word began to spread that something terrible had happened in Aberfan, where her little sister Annette was in class."They didn't really give us any details," she said. Racing off the train, the devastation was clear. "When we looked across to Aberfan, we could just see this black mass."As rescue efforts began, families across the village waited for news. Some of the memories remain too painful to revisit.Image caption, Brothers Kelvin and Malcolm Andrew were the sons of school caretaker Stephen Andrew, whose family still treasure their portraitFor the surviving siblings, that sense of loss seemed to arrive in the most ordinary moments."We always slept together," said Jeanette. "And suddenly I was alone."Denise remembered the same absence."We shared a bed... and then she was gone."Image caption, Paintings of Lynn Harding, Gareth Davies and Terence Davies still hang on the walls of their family homesThe scale of grief was impossible to escape. "In our street, five children were lost in 25 houses," Denise said."Four children died in my street," Jeanette recalled.In an era when grief was rarely discussed openly, many survivors were left to process the tragedy alone.Image source, MirrorpixImage caption, William Richardson made a living as an artist on Llandudno Pier, where he sketched visitors and celebrities including Margaret Thatcher and the Bay City RollersHundreds of miles away in Llandudno, Conwy county, one man was following events in Aberfan on television and in the newspapers.Artist William Richardson had no connection to Aberfan, with his skills being used most often on the pier where he sketched caricatures of visitors and celebrities performing in town.But he was deeply affected by what he saw. According to his children, Jean and Ken, he felt compelled to do something for the bereaved families who had lost their sons and daughters."He saw it on the news and he was so moved by it, he decided to paint them," Jean said."He just wanted to give something back, to show he cared," added Ken.Richardson never sought payment or recognition. Instead, he began creating portraits of children killed in the disaster, working from school photographs and detailed descriptions supplied by parents.Image caption, "It's like looking back at old friends now." Ken and Jean Richardson remember their father's tireless work to complete dozens of paintings for families in Aberfan"The parents would write to him and tell him about the children," Jean said. "What colour their eyes were, their hair, what they wore.""They even sent bits of fabric so he could get it right," Ken added.Jean said her father wanted to capture more than their appearance."He'd ask about their personalities, so he could build that into the painting."Over the years, Richardson is believed to have produced about 100 portraits. As the collection grew, so too did his connection with families in Aberfan.For his children, the portraits became a constant presence."We were surrounded by them for years," said Jean. "All these faces."It's like looking back at old friends now."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, William Richardson (left) was invited to the Wales Office to show some of the portraits to the-then Secretary of State for Wales, George Thomas (second from the right)"We couldn't believe the likeness," Denise said. "That was her."It brought her back to life."Jeanette remembered the effect on her parents when Edwina's portrait arrived."I remember my father crying when the painting came," she said. "If they could have hugged it, they would have."The portraits soon became part of daily life in homes across the village."She was there at Christmas, at parties, always in the room," Denise said of Annette's painting."In our street, every house had one."Image caption, Marylyn and Carl Minett both died in the disasterImage caption, The artist worked from photographs and descriptions of the siblings to create the picturesFor survivors, such as Gaynor Madgwick, who escaped from Pantglas Junior School when the tip collapsed, the images served another purpose."They start conversations," she said. "People begin talking about their children again."For families who had struggled to find the words, the portraits offered a way to keep memories alive."You walked in and their presence was there," Gaynor said.Jeanette agreed: "It was very, very important to us. It felt like she was always with us while it was there."As the generation directly affected by Aberfan grows older, a new question is emerging: what should happen to the portraits?Many remain cherished family possessions. Others have already passed into the care of younger generations, while some have been entrusted to a local museum.Other families have made different choices.Image caption, Denise, Jeanette and Gaynor are concerned about the future of the portraitsGaynor described the heartbreaking decision her family faced after their mother died."Taking them down, you're not taking a painting, you're taking them," she said.The portraits were buried alongside their mother."We buried them with Mam in a white box, like a little coffin."We placed them facing each other."It felt like burying them again."For Jeanette, the future of Edwina's portrait is a source of concern."I worry about what will happen to the painting," she said. "I want people to see them."Denise feels the same pull between preservation and possession."It's a treasure," she said. "I could never part with it."Nearly six decades after the disaster, the paintings remain extraordinary objects. They were created by a man who had never met the children, but his kindness ensured they were treasured by the families who received and loved them.By painstakingly recreating the faces of children who had been lost, William Richardson gave something precious back to a community living with unimaginable grief.For many families, the portraits did more than capture memories. They brought the children home.Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits is available on BBC iPlayer and will be shown on BBC One Wales at 22:40 BST on Monday 19 October

schema.headline: Aberfan disaster: The portraits that helped bring the children home

title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
description: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory fe
body: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year."We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds."We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life."This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia."Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people."They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night."Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said."I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

schema.headline: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car

title: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos
description: Mission set to blast off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonImage source, JAXAImage caption, The spacecraft will head to Mars's larger moon, PhobosBy
body: Mission set to blast off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonImage source, JAXAImage caption, The spacecraft will head to Mars's larger moon, PhobosByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis and Kevin ChurchBBC News Science  Updated 09:03 BSTA space mission is set to launch on Monday that will attempt to grab a piece of Mars' moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth.If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. The spacecraft will blast off from Japan and arrive at Phobos in August 2027.It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. "I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon."The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained."But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity,  and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."Image source, NASAImage caption, Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formedThe rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g."It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.   "However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science.  So it's worth every gram," she said.Image source, JAXAImage caption, The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of PhobosScientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.There are two competing ideas.Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity."When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell."It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly."The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs."One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell."And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars."Image source, Kevin Church/BBC NewsImage caption, Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum  Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists.The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters.But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress.China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031.We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites.These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth.Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water.Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.The MMX mission is scheduled to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Center at 04:41 local time on 20 October (20:41BST 19 October).

schema.headline: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos

title: Kylie Jenner makes Victoria Secret debut in $50 million bra
description: Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra.The make-up mogul s
body: Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra.The make-up mogul surprised the crowd at the lingerie giant's annual show on Sunday while wearing the famed Fantasy Bra, which was made of 18-carat gold and 4,410 diamonds, according to the designer.The Fantasy Bra has been a key feature of the show over the years and wearing it is typically seen as an honour and defining moment for the chosen model.The Kardashians star, 29, being selected to wear the piece delighted some fans, while many others criticised the brand for not giving the opportunity to a veteran supermodel.Social media and marketing expert Joel Marlinarson says the moment was well-engineered and generated "a lot of conversation" on what it means for the "future of modelling and social media". "Of course Kylie represents a new era of celebrity where brands are prioritising who's going to bring the most eyeballs, as opposed to who fits the cookie cutter definition of a model," he tells BBC Newsbeat. Marlinarson says young viewers have a connection with Jenner having grown up watching her on social media and through her reality show with her Kardashian sisters. However, he says there will be a section of the audience who remembers "the iconic Naomi Campbell era of fashion" who might see Jenner being given this moment as a "betrayal of what they know"."Ultimately, this represents this new era of marketing where brands, particularly Victoria's Secret and legacy brands, they don't want to take risks," he says.  "They want to bring in somebody who they know is going to generate eyeballs, who's going to generate those headlines and who can consistently raise a crowd and that's exactly what Victoria's Secret has done."British model Summer Nesbeth tells Newsbeat that she feels Victoria's Secret choosing Jenner was their attempt to keep up with young fans."She's an influencer with a lot of power and we are in the social media age," says the 25-year-old, who has walked the runway at New York Fashion Week.The lingerie brand's catwalk show was scrapped after its 2018 edition drew low ratings, as well as criticism that it was sexist, outdated and lacked diversity.It returned in 2024,  with a promise to "celebrate all women" and featured more a diverse range of talent, including Ashley Graham's appearance as a plus-sized model.Victoria's Secret created this year's Fantasy Bra in collaboration with jewellery brand Jacob & Co, who said it was the "most valuable" one ever created and took 15 artists more than 1,000 hours to create.Nesbeth believes the focus on the bra shows "how detached we are"."People can't eat, people can't afford to keep their lights on," she says. "I think there's a lot of things to say about where we're focussing our attention and where we're putting our money." BBC Newsbeat has contacted Victoria's Secret.

schema.headline: Kylie Jenner makes Victoria Secret debut in $50 million bra

title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and t
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs."A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.The woman is the third complainant the jury have heard from in the trial - and the second to allege rape.The pair had been attending a birthday party in Soho in London in 2004 when the alleged incidents happened.She said after the alleged sexual assault, "The visual I remember is just this big grin - it felt like a clown, (with) that sort of weird look in the eye. It was a normal conversation about him being on Big Brother. He just moved towards (me) and grabbed both my boobs".She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock"."The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said."Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here"."I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."Russell Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

schema.headline: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape

title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
description: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, tha
body: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks  on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with UkraineIvan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome."At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets."When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance."You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets."This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live."In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals."As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."But he argued that his team's actions were justified."I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.Foma did his own digging on Ivan.After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too."The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.Foma has the same rule for his operatives."As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work."Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him."You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag."There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work."Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change."Putin won't live forever," he said.

schema.headline: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
